definition: Truthful and straightforward, especially about something unwelcome; frank.
etymology: From Latin candidus, 'white, pure, sincere', from candere, 'to shine'. The sense moved from whiteness to purity of motive and then to frankness. 'Candle' and 'candidate' (Roman office-seekers wore white togas) share the root.
examples: She gave a candid account of the project's failures, sparing no one, herself included.
To be candid, I do not think the plan will survive its first week.

definition: Well meaning and kindly; disposed to do good to others.
etymology: From Latin benevolens, 'well wishing', from bene, 'well', and velle, 'to wish'. It came into English in the fifteenth century through Old French.
examples: A benevolent neighbour paid the widow's rent through the winter and never mentioned it.
He ruled the firm like a benevolent uncle, indulgent but watchful.

definition: Having or showing a wish to do harm to others.
etymology: From Latin malevolens, 'ill wishing', from male, 'badly', and velle, 'to wish'. It is the exact counterpart of 'benevolent'.
examples: The villain fixed the hero with a malevolent stare and promised he would regret his interference.
Rumour, spread by some malevolent rival, had ruined her reputation before she arrived.

definition: Expressed clearly and easy to understand; also, thinking clearly, especially between periods of confusion.
etymology: From Latin lucidus, 'bright, clear', from lucere, 'to shine', and lux, 'light'.
examples: Her lucid explanation made the tax rules plain even to those of us who dread arithmetic.
In his lucid moments the old man recognised his daughter and asked after the garden.

definition: To make something clear by explaining it.
etymology: From Late Latin elucidare, 'to make clear', from e-, 'out', and lucidus, 'bright'. To elucidate is literally to bring out into the light.
examples: The footnotes elucidate the allusions that a modern reader would otherwise miss.
Asked to elucidate his remark, the minister only made it murkier.

definition: Fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing; clearly expressive of something.
etymology: From Latin eloquens, 'speaking out', from e-, 'out', and loqui, 'to speak'.
examples: Her eloquent plea for the library moved the council to restore its funding.
The empty chair at the table was an eloquent reminder of who was missing.

definition: Tending to talk a great deal; talkative.
etymology: From Latin loquax, 'talkative', from loqui, 'to speak'. The same root gives 'eloquent', 'colloquial' and 'soliloquy'.
examples: Our loquacious driver had told us his life story before we reached the edge of town.
Wine made him loquacious, and he held forth on politics until the candles guttered.

definition: Able to be believed; convincing.
etymology: From Latin credibilis, from credere, 'to believe, to trust'. 'Creed', 'credit' and 'credulous' share the root.
examples: The witness was calm and consistent, and the jury found her entirely credible.
Without a credible plan to repay the loan, the bank would not extend it.

definition: Unwilling or unable to believe something; showing disbelief.
etymology: From Latin incredulus, from in-, 'not', and credulus, 'believing', from credere, 'to believe'. It describes the person who doubts; 'incredible' describes the thing doubted.
examples: He gave an incredulous laugh when told that the cat had opened the refrigerator by itself.
The explorers' tales of a frozen sea met with incredulous silence at court.

definition: The quality of being thankful; readiness to show appreciation for kindness.
etymology: From Medieval Latin gratitudo, from Latin gratus, 'pleasing, thankful'. 'Grateful', 'gratify' and 'grace' come from the same source.
examples: In gratitude for the nurse's care, the family planted a tree outside the ward.
He accepted the gift with a gratitude that embarrassed the giver.

definition: To bring oneself into someone's favour by flattering or trying to please them.
etymology: From Latin in gratiam, 'into favour', from in, 'into', and gratia, 'favour', from gratus, 'pleasing'. Usually used reflexively: one ingratiates oneself with someone.
examples: The new clerk tried to ingratiate himself with the manager by laughing at every joke.
Her ingratiating smile vanished the moment the customer left the shop.

definition: Generous or forgiving, especially towards a rival or someone less powerful.
etymology: From Latin magnanimus, 'great-souled', from magnus, 'great', and animus, 'spirit, mind'. It translates the Greek megalopsychos, a virtue Aristotle praised.
examples: Magnanimous in victory, the champion praised her opponent before mentioning her own win.
It was magnanimous of him to recommend the colleague who had once blocked his promotion.

definition: Calmness and composure, especially in a difficult situation.
etymology: From Latin aequanimitas, from aequus, 'even, level', and animus, 'spirit, mind'. An even mind is one that fortune cannot tilt.
examples: She received the news of her dismissal with such equanimity that her employer was unnerved.
Years at sea had taught him to face storms and calms with the same equanimity.

definition: Lacking courage or resolve; timid.
etymology: From Late Latin pusillanimis, 'small-spirited', from pusillus, 'very small', and animus, 'spirit'. It is the opposite of 'magnanimous' in form as well as meaning.
examples: The committee's pusillanimous refusal to name the culprit satisfied no one.
Too pusillanimous to object aloud, he grumbled about the decision only in private.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation; not clear or decided.
etymology: From Latin ambiguus, 'doubtful', from ambigere, 'to waver, to go about', from ambi-, 'both ways, around', and agere, 'to drive'.
examples: The will was so ambiguous that both brothers believed the house had been left to them.
Her reply, 'We shall see', was deliberately ambiguous.

definition: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something or someone.
etymology: From German Ambivalenz, coined in 1910 by the psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler from Latin ambi-, 'both', and valentia, 'strength', from valere, 'to be strong'. Two feelings pull with equal strength.
morphemes: to be strong, to be worth
examples: He was ambivalent about the promotion: the salary tempted him, but the travel did not.
Many emigrants feel ambivalent towards the country they left, missing it and resenting it at once.

definition: Wary and unwilling to take risks; careful to consider all the circumstances.
etymology: From Latin circumspectus, 'looked around', from circum, 'around', and specere, 'to look'. The circumspect person looks about before acting.
examples: A circumspect investor, she read every page of the prospectus before parting with a penny.
The ambassador was circumspect in his replies, committing his government to nothing.

definition: Having keen insight; quick to notice and understand things that are not obvious.
etymology: From Latin perspicax, 'sharp-sighted', from perspicere, 'to see through', from per, 'through', and specere, 'to look'.
examples: A perspicacious editor, she saw at once that the dull second chapter hid the real beginning of the book.
It took a perspicacious eye to notice that the signature sloped the wrong way.

definition: Conformity to the truth; accuracy. Also, habitual truthfulness.
etymology: From Medieval Latin veracitas, from Latin verax, 'truthful', from verus, 'true'. 'Verify', 'verdict' and 'very' share the root.
examples: The historian doubted the veracity of the diary, since its author was a known boaster.
No one questioned her veracity; in thirty years she had never been caught in a lie.

definition: The appearance of being true or real.
etymology: From Latin verisimilitudo, from verus, 'true', and similis, 'like'. Something with verisimilitude is 'like the truth', whether or not it is true.
examples: The novelist spent a month on a trawler to give her fishing scenes verisimilitude.
A few invented dates and place names lent the forgery an air of verisimilitude.

definition: Holding firmly to something; persistent and not easily giving up.
etymology: From Latin tenax, 'holding fast', from tenere, 'to hold'. 'Tenant', 'tenure' and 'retain' share the root.
examples: The tenacious reporter pursued the story for three years until the minister resigned.
Ivy has a tenacious grip and will pull the mortar from an old wall.

definition: Holding stubbornly to an opinion or course of action, often to an irritating degree.
etymology: From Latin pertinax, from per-, 'thoroughly', and tenax, 'holding fast', from tenere, 'to hold'. It is 'tenacious' intensified, and usually less complimentary.
examples: The pertinacious salesman returned every morning for a week until she bought the encyclopaedia to be rid of him.
He defended his discredited theory with pertinacious zeal long after his colleagues had abandoned it.

definition: Faithfulness to a person, cause or belief; also, the exactness with which something is copied or reproduced.
etymology: From Latin fidelitas, from fidelis, 'faithful', from fides, 'faith, trust'. 'Confide', 'fiancé' and 'bona fide' share the root.
examples: The dog's fidelity to its dead master, waiting each day at the station, became a local legend.
The translation renders the poem with great fidelity, keeping even its awkward rhymes.

definition: Deceitful and untrustworthy; guilty of betraying trust.
etymology: From Latin perfidiosus, from perfidia, 'treachery', from the phrase per fidem (decipere), 'to deceive through trust'. The traitor works by means of the faith placed in him.
examples: The perfidious steward sold his master's secrets to the very men who meant to ruin him.
She never forgave her perfidious friend for repeating what had been told in confidence.

definition: Modest or shy because of a lack of confidence in oneself.
etymology: From Latin diffidens, 'mistrusting', from dis-, 'apart, away', and fidere, 'to trust'. The original English sense was distrust of others; it narrowed to distrust of oneself.
examples: Diffident about her French, she let her husband order for them both.
He offered his opinion in so diffident a murmur that the chairman did not hear it.

definition: To make someone less angry or hostile, especially by giving them something they want.
etymology: From Latin placare, 'to calm, to appease', related to placere, 'to please'. 'Placid' and 'please' are relatives.
examples: The airline tried to placate the stranded passengers with meal vouchers.
Nothing would placate the child but the return of the confiscated drum.

definition: Unable to be appeased or pacified; relentless.
etymology: From Latin implacabilis, from in-, 'not', and placabilis, 'easily calmed', from placare, 'to appease'. The prefix becomes im- before p.
examples: No apology could soften her implacable hatred of the man who had cheated her father.
The tide came on with implacable slowness, and the sandcastle had no chance.

definition: Pleased with oneself or one's situation to the point of ignoring dangers or faults.
etymology: From Latin complacens, 'very pleasing', from com-, an intensifier, and placere, 'to please'. Do not confuse it with 'complaisant', from the same source through French, which means eager to please others.
examples: After ten years without an accident the crew grew complacent and stopped checking the valves.
The champion's complacent smile faded when the newcomer took the first set.

definition: Lasting for a very short time.
etymology: From Greek ephemeros, 'lasting only a day', from epi, 'on', and hemera, 'day'. It was first used in English of fevers that lasted a day, and of the mayfly.
examples: The frost flowers on the window were ephemeral, gone as soon as the sun reached the glass.
Fame built on a single popular song usually proves ephemeral.

definition: Present, appearing or found everywhere.
etymology: From modern Latin ubiquitas, from Latin ubique, 'everywhere', from ubi, 'where'. The noun 'ubiquity' was first a theological term for the omnipresence of Christ.
examples: Plastic bottles are now so ubiquitous that they wash up on beaches no one has ever visited.
In that city the bicycle is ubiquitous; whole streets hold nothing else.

definition: Using very few words.
etymology: From Greek Lakonikos, 'of Laconia', the region whose capital was Sparta. The Spartans were famed for terse speech: threatened by Philip of Macedon with 'If I enter Laconia, I will raze Sparta', they are said to have replied, 'If'.
examples: Asked how the three-day voyage had gone, the laconic captain answered, 'Wet.'
His laconic telegram read only: 'Arrived. Send money.'

definition: Enduring pain or hardship without showing feeling or complaining.
etymology: From Greek Stoikos, from stoa, 'porch': the philosopher Zeno taught at the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch, in Athens around 300 BC. His school held that virtue is the only good and that one should be indifferent to fortune.
examples: She bore the setting of her broken arm with stoic calm, asking only how long it would take.
The villagers met the third flood in five years with a stoic shrug and began to bail.

definition: Subject to sudden and unpredictable changes of mood or mind.
etymology: From Latin mercurialis, 'of Mercury', the swift messenger god. Those born under the planet Mercury were thought lively and changeable, and the quick, restless metal bears the same name.
examples: The orchestra dreaded its mercurial conductor, who might weep at one bar and rage at the next.
Her mercurial enthusiasm settled on pottery in March and had moved to falconry by May.

definition: Extremely idealistic; unrealistic and impractical, especially in pursuit of noble aims.
etymology: From Don Quixote, hero of Cervantes's novel (1605 and 1615), who, his head turned by romances of chivalry, rides out to right wrongs and attacks windmills he takes for giants.
examples: It was a quixotic scheme, to teach Latin to an entire village in a single summer.
His quixotic campaign against the motorway won admiration and four votes.

definition: A person who flatters someone powerful in order to gain advantage.
etymology: From Greek sykophantes, 'informer, slanderer', apparently from sykon, 'fig', and phainein, 'to show'. Why an informer was a 'fig-shower' is uncertain; the ancient explanations are guesses. The modern sense of flatterer arose in English.
examples: Surrounded by sycophants who praised his every whim, the director never learned that the film was a disaster.
She despised the sycophant who agreed with the boss before the boss had finished speaking.

definition: Excessively concerned with minor details or rules, or with displaying learning.
etymology: From 'pedant', which came through French from Italian pedante, 'schoolmaster'. The further origin is uncertain; it may be connected with Latin paedagogus, 'teacher'.
examples: His pedantic insistence on correcting every split infinitive made him unwelcome at the newspaper.
It may sound pedantic, but a tomato is a fruit and the label ought to say so.

definition: Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise.
etymology: From Latin meticulosus, 'fearful', from metus, 'fear'. In English it first meant timid; by the nineteenth century it had come to mean careful as if from fear of error, and today it is a word of praise.
examples: The restorer's meticulous work removed three centuries of varnish without harming a single brushstroke.
He kept meticulous accounts, recording even the price of a box of matches.

definition: Very attentive to accuracy and detail; hard to please, especially about cleanliness or taste.
etymology: From Latin fastidiosus, 'disdainful', from fastidium, 'loathing'. In English it once meant disgusting or disdainful; the sense of exacting taste came later.
examples: Fastidious about his dress, he would not leave the house until his cuffs showed exactly half an inch.
The cat, a fastidious eater, sniffed the cheaper brand and walked away.

definition: Showing great care and perseverance; constant in application.
etymology: From Latin assiduus, 'constantly present', from assidere, 'to sit by', from ad-, 'to', and sedere, 'to sit'. The assiduous worker is the one who stays in the seat.
examples: By assiduous practice of an hour each morning she learned the whole sonata by Easter.
He was an assiduous correspondent, answering every letter on the day it arrived.

definition: Showing dedication and diligence; persistently careful.
etymology: From Latin sedulus, 'zealous, painstaking'. Roman writers derived it from se dolo, 'without guile', and that is the usual account, though not certain. Despite appearances it is not related to sedere, 'to sit'.
examples: With sedulous care the gardener tied each new shoot of the vine to its wire.
She sedulously avoided any mention of the quarrel while her aunt was in the room.

definition: Obedient or attentive to an excessive, servile degree.
etymology: From Latin obsequiosus, 'compliant', from obsequi, 'to comply with', from ob-, 'towards', and sequi, 'to follow'. 'Sequel' and 'consequence' share the root.
examples: The obsequious waiter bowed at every request and agreed that the weather was whatever we said it was.
His obsequious manner towards the wealthy guests contrasted with his rudeness to the staff.

definition: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters.
etymology: From Latin garrulus, 'chattering', from garrire, 'to chatter, to prattle'. The jay's genus, Garrulus, is named for its noise.
examples: The garrulous barber described his nephew's wedding in full before he had finished one sideburn.
Age had made the colonel garrulous, and every campaign was fought again over the soup.

definition: Reserved or uncommunicative in speech; saying little by habit.
etymology: From Latin taciturnus, from tacitus, 'silent', from tacere, 'to be silent'. 'Tacit', meaning understood without being said, is from the same verb.
examples: The taciturn shepherd answered our questions with nods and spoke perhaps ten words all afternoon.
Normally taciturn, she surprised the table by telling a long and very funny story.

definition: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily; reserved about a particular matter.
etymology: From Latin reticens, 'keeping silent', from reticere, from re-, an intensifier, and tacere, 'to be silent'. Where 'taciturn' describes a temperament, 'reticent' usually describes silence on a subject.
examples: He talked freely about his travels but was reticent about the years he had spent in prison.
Her reticence on the subject of her family led to a good deal of idle speculation.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation, often deliberately so; uncertain or questionable in nature.
etymology: From Late Latin aequivocus, 'of equal voice', from aequus, 'equal', and vocare, 'to call', from vox, 'voice'. An equivocal statement speaks with two voices at once.
examples: Pressed on whether taxes would rise, the candidate gave an equivocal answer about 'all options'.
The results of the trial were equivocal: some patients improved, and as many grew worse.

definition: Expressing opinions or feelings in a loud and forceful way.
etymology: From Latin vociferari, 'to shout', from vox, 'voice', and ferre, 'to carry'. The vociferous carry their voices far.
examples: Vociferous protests from the gallery forced the speaker to stop three times.
The plan's most vociferous critic had not, it emerged, read it.

definition: Tending to cause sleep; tediously dull.
etymology: From Latin sopor, 'deep sleep', and -ficus, 'making', from facere, 'to make'.
examples: The warm room and the lecturer's soporific drone had half the audience nodding by three o'clock.
A heavy lunch has a soporific effect that no amount of coffee quite undoes.

definition: Sleepy or drowsy; also, quiet and inactive as if asleep.
etymology: From Latin somnolentus, from somnus, 'sleep'. 'Insomnia' and 'somnambulist', a sleepwalker, share the root.
examples: The somnolent guard did not stir as the cat walked across his desk.
It was a somnolent little town where the loudest sound at noon was the church clock.

definition: Proceeding in a gradual, subtle way but with harmful effect.
etymology: From Latin insidiosus, 'cunning', from insidiae, 'an ambush', from insidere, 'to sit in wait', from in-, 'in', and sedere, 'to sit'.
examples: Damp is an insidious enemy of old books, doing its damage for years before a stain appears.
The insidious habit of checking his telephone had eaten two hours of every day before he noticed.

definition: Having a harmful effect, especially in a gradual or subtle way; destructive.
etymology: From Latin perniciosus, 'destructive', from pernicies, 'ruin', from per-, 'thoroughly', and nex, 'violent death'.
examples: The pernicious rumour that the bank was failing caused the very run that ruined it.
She thought flattery a pernicious influence on a young writer, worse than any harsh review.

definition: Too great, extreme or sacred to be expressed in words.
etymology: From Latin ineffabilis, from in-, 'not', and effabilis, 'able to be uttered', from effari, 'to speak out', from ex-, 'out', and fari, 'to speak'.
examples: Standing under the dome at dawn she felt an ineffable peace that she never managed to describe.
There was an ineffable sadness in the tune, though no one could say which notes held it.

definition: Impossible to stop or prevent; not to be moved by pleading.
etymology: From Latin inexorabilis, from in-, 'not', and exorabilis, 'able to be moved by entreaty', from exorare, 'to prevail upon', from ex-, 'out', and orare, 'to plead, to pray'.
examples: The glacier's inexorable advance, a few feet each year, at last swallowed the abandoned hut.
The judge was inexorable, and no plea from the prisoner's mother altered the sentence.

definition: Stubbornly uncooperative towards authority or discipline.
etymology: From Latin recalcitrare, 'to kick back', from re-, 'back', and calcitrare, 'to kick', from calx, 'heel'. The image is of a mule lashing out at its driver.
examples: The recalcitrant pupil folded his arms and refused to open the book, whatever the punishment.
After an hour with a recalcitrant lock, she gave up and climbed in through the window.

definition: Noisy and difficult to control.
etymology: From Latin obstreperus, 'clamorous', from obstrepere, 'to make a noise against', from ob-, 'against', and strepere, 'to make a noise'.
examples: Two obstreperous guests were shouting over the toasts until the bride's uncle led them outside.
The class grew obstreperous on the last afternoon of term, and no lesson was possible.

definition: Carried out with a minimum of effort or thought, merely as a duty.
etymology: From Late Latin perfunctorius, 'careless', from perfungi, 'to get through, to discharge', from per-, 'through', and fungi, 'to perform'. 'Function' shares the root.
examples: The customs officer gave our bags a perfunctory glance and waved us through.
His apology was so perfunctory, mumbled without looking up, that it made matters worse.

definition: Lacking a plan, purpose or enthusiasm; passing aimlessly from one thing to another.
etymology: From Latin desultorius, 'of a desultor', a circus rider who leapt from one galloping horse to another, from desilire, 'to leap down', from de-, 'down', and salire, 'to leap'.
examples: After a few desultory attempts to tidy the attic, he sat down on a trunk and read old letters.
The conversation was desultory, drifting from the weather to the price of coal and back.

definition: Optimistic, especially in a difficult situation.
etymology: From Latin sanguineus, 'of blood', from sanguis, 'blood'. In the old medicine of the four humours, a person in whom blood predominated was ruddy, courageous and hopeful.
examples: Despite two failed harvests, the farmer remained sanguine about the coming year.
I am less sanguine than you that the bridge will be finished before winter.

definition: Having a calm, unemotional temperament; not easily excited.
etymology: From Greek phlegmatikos, from phlegma, 'inflammation', later the humour phlegm, from phlegein, 'to burn'. In the theory of the four humours an excess of phlegm made a person sluggish and cool.
examples: The phlegmatic pilot announced the engine failure in the tone of a man reading a bus timetable.
Nothing ruffled her phlegmatic husband, not even the news that the roof had blown off.

definition: Looking or sounding sad and dismal, often in an exaggerated way.
etymology: From Latin lugubris, 'mournful', from lugere, 'to mourn'.
examples: The bloodhound's lugubrious face suggested a grief that its wagging tail denied.
In a lugubrious voice the butler informed us that the picnic had been rained off.

definition: The partly shaded region around the darkest part of a shadow; figuratively, an area of uncertainty or partial obscurity surrounding something.
etymology: Modern Latin, coined by the astronomer Johannes Kepler in 1604 from Latin paene, 'almost', and umbra, 'shadow'. 'Peninsula', almost an island, is formed the same way.
examples: During the partial eclipse our town lay in the penumbra, and the afternoon merely dimmed.
Around the few facts of the poet's life there is a wide penumbra of legend.
